blocks.text: Silent Push is a preemptive cyber defence platform that maps attacker infrastructure before it is used in an attack. Its Indicators of Future Attack (IOFA) are built from DNS, web content, certificate and WHOIS data, so security teams can block threats earlier. Evanssion distributes Silent Push across the Middle East and Africa.

Most threat feeds report infrastructure after an attack has already used it. Silent Push looks at how attackers build and configure their servers, then flags matching infrastructure that has been set up but not yet used. Teams get that intelligence through a console, feeds and an API.

items: Threat hunting: pivot from one indicator to related attacker infrastructure using live and historic DNS, web content and certificate data.
Indicators of Future Attack (IOFA) feeds for blocking and enrichment in existing security tools.
Brand protection: find and counter impersonation domains aimed at your customers or staff.
Tracking of command-and-control infrastructure and advanced persistent threat (APT) activity.
Automated intelligence delivered by API for SIEM, SOAR and TIP integration.

blocks.text: SOC managers, incident response teams and cyber threat intelligence analysts. The vendor lists financial services firms, national CERT teams, defence contractors and ISAC intelligence teams among its customers. In our region the natural fit is banks, telecoms, government-linked entities and large enterprises with a dedicated security operations team.

Built on live and historic DNS, web content scanning, certificate and WHOIS data, plus first-party enrichment.

items.q: What is an Indicator of Future Attack?
items.a: An Indicator of Future Attack (IOFA) is a signal that a piece of internet infrastructure, such as a domain or IP address, matches the pattern attackers use to prepare an attack, before any attack has used it. Silent Push uses IOFA so that defenders can block infrastructure ahead of time.

items.q: How is this different from an indicator of compromise feed?
items.a: Indicators of compromise usually describe infrastructure already seen in an attack. Silent Push aims to identify attacker-built infrastructure earlier, from how it is configured, so the block can come before the first hit.

items.q: Which teams use Silent Push?
items.a: Mainly SOC, incident response and threat intelligence teams. Brand protection and fraud teams also use it to find impersonation domains.

items.a: Contact Evanssion for a briefing and a trial discussion. We work directly with enterprises and through registered partners.

blocks.text: ReversingLabs is a software supply chain security and malware analysis company. items.q: What is software supply chain security?
items.a: It is the practice of verifying that the software you build or buy has not been tampered with and does not contain malware, secrets or exploitable flaws. It covers your own builds, third-party software and open-source dependencies.

blocks.text: Illumio is a breach containment platform. It combines segmentation, which limits what each workload and device can talk to, with detection and response based on an AI security graph, so an attacker who gets in cannot move freely. Evanssion distributes Illumio in the Middle East and Africa.

Prevention will not stop every attack, so the aim is to limit the damage. Illumio maps how workloads communicate across data centres, cloud and endpoints, then applies policy that blocks the paths an attacker would use for lateral movement.

items.q: What is microsegmentation?
items.a: Microsegmentation divides a network into small zones with their own rules, down to individual workloads, so that a compromised system cannot freely reach others.

spec.Schema: Organization (vendor), Service or Product, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList

blocks.text: Backflipt Lumen is a platform that governs enterprise AI agents. It discovers every agent and the resources it can reach, decides what each agent may do at the moment it acts, and issues short-lived credentials so agents never hold permanent secrets. It deploys in your own VPC or on-premises. Evanssion distributes Backflipt in the Middle East and Africa.

Agents talk to each other and to tools through protocols such as A2A and MCP. Backflipt treats the problem as two decisions made in the path of the traffic: intent, checked by the Lumen A2A Gateway, and credentials, handled by the POET Credential Broker.

items: Agent discovery with risk scores, including agents nobody registered.
Lumen A2A Gateway: inline inspection of agent-to-agent and agent-to-MCP traffic, with Smart Policies and PeerGroups.
POET Credential Broker: time-bound, workload-bound tokens in place of standing secrets.
Agent-ready applications: generate MCP servers and A2A agents from existing APIs (OpenAPI, Swagger, RAML) without code.
Lumen AI TransferView with Galileo: visibility and SLA alerts for governed file transfers.

blocks.text: Enterprises that are deploying agents from several platforms and need identity, authorisation and audit for non-human actors. Security architects, identity teams and platform teams are the main buyers.

spec.Meta description: Secure how your organisation uses AI: visibility, policy control and protection for employees, applications and AI agents. Solutions via Evanssion in the Gulf.

blocks.text: AI security and governance is the set of controls that show how AI is used in your organisation, apply policy to that use, and protect AI systems from attack. It covers staff using public AI tools, AI applications you build, and autonomous agents that act on your behalf.

AI adoption usually starts in the business, not in security. Employees paste company data into public tools, teams connect agents to internal systems, and developers add language models to applications. Each of these creates data, access and compliance risk, and most organisations cannot yet say what AI is in use or what it can reach.

items: A live inventory of AI tools, models, applications, agents and MCP servers.
Policies by role and intent that allow approved use and block risky use.
Protection against prompt injection, jailbreaks and data leakage at runtime.
Identity and least-privilege access for agents, with short-lived credentials.
Audit trails and reports that stand up to regulators.

items.q: What is shadow AI?
items.a: Shadow AI is any AI tool, model or agent used in an organisation without security or IT approval, such as an employee using a public chatbot with company data.

items.q: What is prompt injection?
items.a: Prompt injection is an attack where crafted input makes an AI model ignore its instructions or reveal data. It is one of the main risks for AI applications and agents.

items.q: Who should own AI governance?
items.a: It is shared. Security sets controls, compliance maps them to regulation, and the business owns the use cases. A platform that gives all three the same view makes this practical.

blocks.text: Application security finds and fixes flaws in the software you build before attackers can use them. Modern programmes test running applications and APIs, validate which findings can really be exploited, and feed the confirmed ones to developers in the tools they already use.

Teams run many scanners and receive long lists of findings, most of which are never fixed. AI coding assistants add code faster than reviewers can check it. Developers lose trust in tools that raise false alarms, and real flaws wait in the queue.

items.q: What is the difference between SAST and DAST?
items.a: Static testing (SAST) reads source code without running it. Dynamic testing (DAST) probes a running application like an attacker. Most programmes use both.

items.q: What is ASPM?
items.a: Application security posture management brings findings from many tools into one place, ranks them by risk and tracks them to closure.

items.q: Do we need to test APIs separately?
items.a: APIs expose business logic and data directly, so they need their own testing. Good tools discover and test APIs as part of the same workflow.

blocks.text: Threat intelligence tells security teams who is attacking, how, and with what. The most useful intelligence is early and specific: it flags attacker infrastructure before it is used, and it adds context to alerts so analysts can decide faster.

Many feeds list indicators after an attack has already used them. By then the phishing email has been delivered and the malware has called home. Teams need intelligence that arrives earlier, connects related infrastructure, and plugs straight into the tools they run.

items.q: What is a software supply chain attack?
items.a: It is an attack that compromises software at a supplier, in a library or in a build process, so that the malicious code reaches many customers through a trusted update.

items.q: What is an SBOM?
items.a: A software bill of materials lists the components in a piece of software. It is useful, but it does not prove the software is free of malware or tampering.

items.q: Does this apply to us if we do not develop software?
items.a: Yes. Any organisation that runs third-party software depends on its suppliers' build processes. Assessing vendor software is part of the answer.

blocks.text: Vulnerability and exposure management is the work of finding weaknesses, deciding which ones matter, and fixing them quickly. The hard part is rarely finding them. It is merging many lists, ranking by real risk, and getting fixes deployed.

Each scanner has its own list. The same flaw appears several times, severity scores ignore whether an exploit exists, and patching waits on tickets and maintenance windows. Auditors then ask for evidence that the process works.

items: One consolidated record across scanners and teams.
Ranking that uses exploit data such as EPSS and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list.
Remediation SLAs that are measured, not estimated.
Automated patching with verification.

items.a: It ranks vulnerabilities by the likelihood and impact of real attacks, using exploit data and asset importance, rather than by severity score alone.

items.q: What are EPSS and CISA KEV?
items.a: The Exploit Prediction Scoring System estimates the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited. The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue lists flaws that are being exploited now.

items.q: Should patching be automatic?
items.a: For most endpoint and third-party software, yes, within policy and approved windows. Critical servers often need change control.

name: Breach containment and Zero Trust segmentation

spec.Meta description: Stop attackers moving once they are inside. Microsegmentation and breach containment for hybrid and multi-cloud estates, via Evanssion in the Gulf.
spec.H1: Breach containment and Zero Trust segmentation

blocks.text: Breach containment limits how far an attacker can move after getting in. By mapping which systems need to talk to each other and blocking everything else, segmentation turns a breach of one server into an incident, rather than a crisis across the whole estate.

Perimeter controls cannot stop every attack. Once inside, ransomware and intruders move laterally across flat networks, hybrid clouds and shared services. Organisations need to see how workloads communicate and enforce rules that limit those paths.

items: A live map of how workloads and devices communicate.
Policy that limits traffic to what is needed, across data centre and cloud.
Quick isolation of an affected workload during an incident.
Detection of unusual lateral movement.
Evidence of segmentation for audits and Zero Trust programmes.

items.q: What is lateral movement?
items.a: Lateral movement is how attackers move from the first system they compromise to others in the network in search of valuable data or systems.

items.q: How is segmentation different from a firewall?
items.a: Perimeter firewalls control traffic at the edge. Segmentation controls traffic between workloads inside the network and cloud, down to individual systems.

items.q: Is this part of Zero Trust?
items.a: Yes. Limiting access to what is explicitly needed, and assuming a breach is possible, are core Zero Trust principles.

spec.Page type: Glossary hub (plus one page per term, /insights/glossary/term-name/)
spec.Meta description: Plain-language definitions of cybersecurity and AI security terms, from ASPM and microsegmentation to MCP and prompt injection.

blocks.text: Short, plain definitions of the terms our vendors and customers use. Each term has its own page so search engines and AI assistants can cite it directly.

head: Term
Definition (40 to 60 words, ready to publish after review)
rows: Application security posture management brings findings from code, build, cloud and runtime scanners into one view, removes duplicates, ranks them by real risk and tracks fixes to closure.
Shadow AI is any AI tool, model or agent used inside an organisation without security or IT approval, such as an employee pasting company data into a public chatbot.
Prompt injection is an attack in which crafted input makes an AI model ignore its instructions, reveal data or take unintended actions. It is a leading risk for AI applications and agents.
Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets AI agents connect to tools and data sources. Each MCP server an agent can reach extends what the agent can do, so access needs to be governed.
Agent2Agent is a protocol that lets AI agents from different platforms communicate and delegate tasks to each other. Security teams need to authenticate and authorise this traffic.

An Indicator of Future Attack is a signal that internet infrastructure matches the pattern attackers use to prepare an attack, before any attack has used it. Silent Push uses IOFA for preemptive defence.

Software supply chain security verifies that software you build or buy has not been tampered with and does not hide malware, secrets or exploitable flaws, including in open-source and third-party components.
Microsegmentation divides a network or cloud into small zones with their own rules, down to individual workloads, so a compromised system cannot freely reach others.
Lateral movement is how an attacker moves from the first system they compromise to others in the environment, looking for credentials, data or systems to control.
A security data fabric collects, cleans, enriches and routes security and observability data to the tools that need it, reducing cost and improving detection quality.
An AI SOC uses AI agents to perform security operations work such as alert triage, investigation and threat hunting, with analysts reviewing and deciding on important cases.
A value-added distributor sells technology through channel partners and adds services such as technical enablement, presales, training and local support, beyond simply supplying product.
